Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Infection can cause symptoms ranging from mild fever and headache to more severe complications that may require hospitalization. As dengue remains a major public health concern in Sri Lanka, continuous surveillance is important for identifying outbreaks, monitoring transmission patterns, and supporting public health interventions.

This dashboard provides an interactive exploration of weekly dengue surveillance data reported across Sri Lanka through the denguedatahub package. The visualizations allow users to examine national trends, compare districts, investigate seasonal patterns, explore geographic variation, and review historical dengue serotype information.

  • Overview provides a summary of the national dengue situation and key surveillance indicators.
  • National Trends displays long-term patterns in dengue incidence and compares annual case burdens across high-incidence districts.
  • Trend & Seasonality presents an STL decomposition that separates observed dengue incidence into long-term trend, recurring seasonal patterns, and irregular variation.
  • District Explorer allows users to explore weekly dengue trajectories for individual districts using a dropdown selector, with a zoomable range slider for fine-grained time navigation.
  • Spatial Distribution visualizes the geographic distribution of annual dengue cases across Sri Lanka & a heatmap of how the dengue cases spread across the years in Sri Lanka.
  • Serotypes shows the historical circulation of dengue virus serotypes reported in Sri Lanka.
  • Data provides access to the surveillance records and serotype data used throughout the dashboard.

Data are obtained from the denguedatahub R package, developed by Dr. Thiyanga Talagala and collaborators.

STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess) separates the observed dengue case series into three components: a long-term trend, recurring seasonal patterns, and an irregular remainder. This helps identify underlying transmission patterns that may not be immediately visible in the raw data.
